title: The Five Kingdoms Research Station
subtitle: Eight real specimens just arrived. Only real evidence — never appearance — decides which kingdom each one belongs to.

learningFocus.summary: In this activity students practise the opening classification content of IGCSE Biology (Edexcel), Topic 1b: Variety of Living Organisms, by running real diagnostic tests — cell type, cell wall material and nutrition mode — on real photographs of eight organisms (including two genuine microscope specimens) and sorting each into its correct kingdom. Beyond the five-kingdom system itself, the activity builds the classification and evidence-based reasoning skills that underpin every later IGCSE Biology topic, from cell biology to the role of bacteria in disease and biotechnology, and trains students to resist classifying by appearance alone — the exact misconception (mistaking coral for a plant, or seaweed for a true plant) that examiners repeatedly test.

orient.objective: Classify real organisms into the five kingdoms — Plants, Animals, Fungi, Protoctista and Bacteria — using their cell type, cell wall and nutrition, not their appearance.
orient.courseLink: This is the opening classification content of IGCSE Biology (Edexcel) Topic 1: The Nature and Variety of Living Organisms. Every organism you study for the rest of this course — from photosynthesising plants to disease-causing bacteria — first has to be placed correctly into one of these five kingdoms.
orient.mission: A crate of eight unlabelled specimens has just arrived at your research station. Two are real microscope slides. The rest are field photographs — including one that looks like seaweed but isn't a plant, and one that looks like a plant but is actually an animal. Your job: run real diagnostic tests on each one and sort it into its correct kingdom, using evidence, not guesswork.
steps: Meet the five kingdoms by tapping each one in the classification chart.
Predict which kingdoms you think are eukaryotic before you test anything.
Scan two real microscope specimens to see a nucleus — and its absence — for yourself.
Run diagnostic tests on eight real specimens and sort each into its kingdom.
Explain, apply, then answer the Knowledge Check.
Generate your Learning Evidence to hand in.
orient.realLife: Every mushroom on a pizza, the bacteria that turn milk into yoghurt, the seaweed wrapped around a sushi roll and the coral reef tourists travel to see all belong to different kingdoms — food scientists, doctors and conservationists all depend on classifying organisms like these correctly, and get it wrong at their peril.
successCriteria: You can name the five kingdoms and state which are eukaryotic and which are prokaryotic.
You can use cell type, cell wall material and nutrition mode to classify a real organism you have never seen before.
You can explain why an organism that looks like a plant or animal might actually belong to a completely different kingdom.
orient.scientificObservation: Eight unlabelled specimens are on the bench: several clearly look like plants or animals, one looks like a plant but lives entirely underwater, one looks like a plant but is actually a colony of animals, and two can only be identified through a microscope.
orient.scientificQuestion: What real, testable features actually decide which kingdom an organism belongs to — not just what it looks like at first glance?

predict.prompt: Before you scan anything: which of these five kingdoms do you predict are eukaryotic (their cells have a nucleus)?
predict.hint: Choose as many as you think apply. You'll revisit this after Investigate.

investigate.title: The Classification Research Station
investigate.lede: First scan two real microscope specimens to see a nucleus — and its absence — with your own eyes. Then run diagnostic tests on eight real specimens and sort each one into its correct kingdom.

record.intro: Every diagnostic scan and every classification decision is logged here automatically as you work.
record.emptyText: No results yet. Start scanning specimens in the Investigate stage.

_markingScheme_note: REQUIRED reproducible marking (CLAUDE.md §5). markingScheme replaces the old flat expectedPoints array. One entry per available mark: 'marks' (usually 1), 'criterion' (the specific, assessable thing that earns it — not a vague theme), 'accept' (acceptable alternative/equivalent wording, so the marker doesn't require exact keywords), 'insufficient' (a common response that looks right but doesn't earn the mark, where useful), and 'dependsOn' (0-based index of another point in THIS array that must also be met, or omit/null if independent). maxMarks must equal the sum of markingScheme[].marks.

explain.prompt: Using your results, explain why bacteria are placed in a completely separate kingdom from the other four — even though some bacteria, like plants, can photosynthesise.
explain.lede: Refer to specific specimens from your Investigation Record, not just 'they look different'.

markingScheme.criterion: States that the deciding feature is cell type: bacteria cells are prokaryotic (no nucleus; genetic material free in the cytoplasm), while all four other kingdoms are eukaryotic (a nucleus enclosed in a membrane).
markingScheme.accept: 'No nucleus' for prokaryotic and 'has a nucleus' for eukaryotic are acceptable without the technical terms.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why nutrition mode cannot be the deciding feature, because it varies within kingdoms too (e.g. some bacteria photosynthesise like plants; fungi and protoctista also feed in different ways), yet organisms are still grouped by cell type first.
markingScheme.insufficient: Restating 'bacteria feed differently' without explaining why nutrition varies within kingdoms and so cannot be the deciding feature.

markingScheme.criterion: Refers to their own Investigation Record evidence: the bacteria specimen showed no visible nucleus under the microscope while the amoeba (a eukaryote) clearly showed one, and states this is the same prokaryote/eukaryote split separating Bacteria from every other kingdom.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct reference to their own two microscope specimen results, even if not word-for-word.
markingScheme.insufficient: Mentioning the microscope specimens without stating what was or wasn't seen (the nucleus).

apply.prompt: A scientist discovers a new, unicellular microorganism. It has no nucleus, but it can photosynthesise using pigments in its cytoplasm. Which kingdom should it be classified into, and why?
apply.lede: Think about which single feature outweighs everything else when it comes to sorting an organism into a kingdom.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies the kingdom as Bacteria, because the organism has no nucleus (it is prokaryotic).
markingScheme.insufficient: Naming any other kingdom, or naming Bacteria with no reason given.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that being able to photosynthesise does not override this: real bacteria (cyanobacteria) photosynthesise in exactly this way and are still classified as Bacteria because they lack a nucleus.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct example (real or reasoned) showing that nutrition mode does not override cell type.

markingScheme.criterion: States explicitly that cell type (not nutrition mode) is the general deciding evidence for classification, ideally naming this as the same reasoning microbiologists use for newly discovered microorganisms.
markingScheme.insufficient: Repeating 'no nucleus = Bacteria' without stating the general rule that cell type outweighs nutrition mode.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which single feature is used to decide whether an organism belongs to the Bacteria kingdom rather than one of the other four kingdoms?

options.label: Whether the cell has a nucleus (prokaryotic vs eukaryotic)
Whether the organism has a cell wall

knowledgeCheck.explain: Bacteria are the only kingdom that is prokaryotic — their cells have no nucleus. Some protoctista are also unicellular, some organisms in several kingdoms can move, and cell walls appear in three of the five kingdoms, so none of those features are unique to Bacteria.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which cell wall material is found in fungi but never in plants?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin — the same tough material found in insect exoskeletons. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, and peptidoglycan is found only in bacterial cell walls.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each kingdom to how it gets its food (its mode of nutrition).

pairs.right: Autotrophic — make their own food by photosynthesis
Saprophytic — feed on dead or decaying matter using extracellular enzymes

knowledgeCheck.explain: These are the three classic nutrition modes tested at IGCSE — but remember from Explain and Apply that nutrition mode alone can never be used to identify the Bacteria kingdom, since some bacteria photosynthesise and others feed in other ways.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Coral polyps have no cell wall, cannot photosynthesise, and catch and digest tiny floating organisms with stinging tentacles. Even though a coral colony can look like an underwater plant, which kingdom is it actually classified into?
knowledgeCheck.explain: No cell wall and heterotrophic feeding (catching and digesting other organisms) are both classic animal features — coral is a colony of tiny animals, whatever its plant-like appearance suggests.

rubric.note: You are graded out of the total marks, shown as a percentage.

criteria.label: Knowledge & understanding
criteria.source: Auto-marked from the Knowledge Check (auto_marked_score) — the teacher does not mark this row.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.source: = the Explain question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (cell type identified, nutrition mode ruled out, own microscope specimens cited). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: No specimens or evidence from the Investigation Record referenced.
Mentions a specimen or feature but does not connect it to the claim being made.
Refers to specific specimens from the Investigation Record and links them to the claim, with a minor gap.
Clearly cites specific specimens and diagnostic features from the Investigation Record and uses them precisely to justify the classification.

criteria.label: Scientific reasoning
criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (correct kingdom named, photosynthesis-overridden argument, general cell-type rule stated). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: No attempt to reason about why cell type outweighs nutrition mode.
States a conclusion (e.g. 'it is Bacteria') but does not explain why.
Explains why, with one gap in the scientific logic (e.g. not addressing why nutrition mode is misleading).
Explains fully and correctly why cell type (prokaryotic vs eukaryotic), not nutrition mode, is the deciding evidence.

criteria.label: Communication
criteria.source: Assessed holistically across BOTH the Explain and Apply answers together — independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Unclear or missing sentences; no scientific terms.
Understandable but with unclear phrasing or missing key terms.
Clear, well-formed sentences using correct scientific vocabulary (e.g. 'prokaryotic', 'eukaryotic', 'heterotrophic').

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's markingScheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain markingScheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply markingScheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. The Knowledge Check is already auto-marked in auto_marked_score — copy it into knowledge_accuracy (6 marks = full). Accept scientifically valid alternative wording (e.g. 'has no nucleus' for 'prokaryotic', 'makes its own food' for 'autotrophic'). Do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 11 (6 auto + 3 + 3 + 2); report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.

es.title: La Estación de Investigación de los Cinco Reinos
es.subtitle: Ocho especímenes reales acaban de llegar. Solo la evidencia real —nunca el aspecto— decide a qué reino pertenece cada uno.
es.module: Tema 1b: Variedad de los seres vivos

learningFocus.summary: En esta actividad, los estudiantes practican el contenido inicial de clasificación de Biología IGCSE (Edexcel), Tema 1b: Variedad de los seres vivos, realizando pruebas diagnósticas reales —tipo de célula, material de la pared celular y modo de nutrición— sobre fotografías reales de ocho organismos (incluidas dos muestras reales de microscopio) y clasificando cada uno en su reino correcto. Además del sistema de los cinco reinos, la actividad desarrolla las destrezas de clasificación y razonamiento basado en evidencia que sustentan todos los temas posteriores de Biología IGCSE, desde la biología celular hasta el papel de las bacterias en la enfermedad y la biotecnología, y entrena a los estudiantes a no clasificar solo por apariencia —exactamente el error que confunde el coral con una planta, o las algas con una planta verdadera— que los examinadores ponen a prueba repetidamente.

orient.objective: Clasificar organismos reales en los cinco reinos —Plantas, Animales, Hongos, Protoctistas y Bacterias— usando su tipo de célula, pared celular y nutrición, no su apariencia.
orient.courseLink: Este es el contenido inicial de clasificación del Tema 1 de Biología IGCSE (Edexcel): La naturaleza y variedad de los seres vivos. Todo organismo que estudies en el resto de este curso —desde plantas que fotosintetizan hasta bacterias causantes de enfermedades— primero debe ubicarse correctamente en uno de estos cinco reinos.
orient.mission: Acaba de llegar a tu estación de investigación una caja con ocho especímenes sin etiquetar. Dos son portaobjetos de microscopio reales. El resto son fotografías de campo —incluida una que parece un alga pero no es una planta, y otra que parece una planta pero en realidad es un animal. Tu tarea: realizar pruebas diagnósticas reales sobre cada uno y clasificarlo en su reino correcto, usando evidencia, no suposiciones.
steps: Conoce los cinco reinos tocando cada uno en el esquema de clasificación.
Predice qué reinos crees que son eucariotas antes de probar nada.
Escanea dos especímenes reales de microscopio para ver un núcleo —y su ausencia— con tus propios ojos.
Realiza pruebas diagnósticas sobre ocho especímenes reales y clasifica cada uno en su reino.
Explica, aplica y responde la Comprobación de conocimientos.
Genera tu Evidencia de Aprendizaje para entregar.
orient.realLife: Cada champiñón de una pizza, las bacterias que convierten la leche en yogur, el alga que envuelve un rollo de sushi y el arrecife de coral que los turistas viajan a ver pertenecen a reinos distintos —científicos de alimentos, médicos y conservacionistas dependen de clasificar organismos como estos correctamente, y se equivocan bajo su propio riesgo.
successCriteria: Puedes nombrar los cinco reinos e indicar cuáles son eucariotas y cuáles procariotas.
Puedes usar el tipo de célula, el material de la pared celular y el modo de nutrición para clasificar un organismo real que nunca has visto.
Puedes explicar por qué un organismo que parece una planta o un animal podría en realidad pertenecer a un reino completamente distinto.

predict.prompt: Antes de escanear nada: ¿cuáles de estos cinco reinos predices que son eucariotas (sus células tienen núcleo)?
predict.hint: Elige todos los que creas que aplican. Volverás a esto después de Investigar.

investigate.title: La Estación de Investigación de Clasificación
investigate.lede: Primero escanea dos especímenes reales de microscopio para ver un núcleo —y su ausencia— con tus propios ojos. Luego realiza pruebas diagnósticas sobre ocho especímenes reales y clasifica cada uno en su reino correcto.

record.intro: Cada escaneo diagnóstico y cada decisión de clasificación se registra aquí automáticamente mientras trabajas.
record.emptyText: Todavía no hay resultados. Empieza a escanear especímenes en la etapa Investigar.

explain.prompt: Usando tus resultados, explica por qué las bacterias se ubican en un reino completamente separado de los otros cuatro —aunque algunas bacterias, como las plantas, puedan fotosintetizar.
explain.lede: Haz referencia a especímenes concretos de tu Registro de investigación, no solo a que 'se ven diferentes'.

apply.prompt: Una científica descubre un nuevo microorganismo unicelular. No tiene núcleo, pero puede fotosintetizar usando pigmentos en su citoplasma. ¿En qué reino debería clasificarse, y por qué?
apply.lede: Piensa en qué característica por sí sola pesa más que todas las demás a la hora de clasificar un organismo en un reino.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: ¿Qué característica única se usa para decidir si un organismo pertenece al reino Bacterias en lugar de a uno de los otros cuatro reinos?

options.label: Si la célula tiene núcleo (procariota frente a eucariota)
Si el organismo tiene pared celular

knowledgeCheck.explain: Las bacterias son el único reino procariota —sus células no tienen núcleo. Algunos protoctistas también son unicelulares, organismos de varios reinos pueden moverse, y la pared celular aparece en tres de los cinco reinos, así que ninguna de esas características es exclusiva de las bacterias.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: ¿Qué material de la pared celular se encuentra en los hongos pero nunca en las plantas?

options.label: Los hongos no tienen pared celular

knowledgeCheck.explain: Las paredes celulares de los hongos están hechas de quitina —el mismo material resistente del exoesqueleto de los insectos. Las paredes celulares de las plantas están hechas de celulosa, y el peptidoglicano se encuentra solo en las paredes celulares bacterianas.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Relaciona cada reino con su modo de nutrición.

pairs.right: Autótrofas — fabrican su propio alimento mediante la fotosíntesis
Heterótrofos — se alimentan de otros organismos
Saprófitos — se alimentan de materia muerta o en descomposición usando enzimas extracelulares

knowledgeCheck.explain: Estos son los tres modos de nutrición clásicos evaluados en IGCSE —pero recuerda de Explicar y Aplicar que el modo de nutrición por sí solo nunca puede usarse para identificar el reino Bacterias, ya que algunas bacterias fotosintetizan y otras se alimentan de otras formas.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Los pólipos de coral no tienen pared celular, no pueden fotosintetizar, y atrapan y digieren pequeños organismos flotantes con tentáculos urticantes. Aunque una colonia de coral pueda parecer una planta submarina, ¿en qué reino se clasifica realmente?
knowledgeCheck.explain: La ausencia de pared celular y la alimentación heterótrofa (atrapar y digerir otros organismos) son características animales clásicas —el coral es una colonia de pequeños animales, sin importar lo que sugiera su aspecto parecido a una planta.

rubric.note: Tu nota son los puntos que obtienes del total, como porcentaje.

levels.descriptor: No se menciona ningún espécimen ni evidencia del Registro de investigación.
Menciona un espécimen o característica pero no lo relaciona con la afirmación.
Se refiere a especímenes concretos del Registro de investigación y los relaciona con la afirmación, con un pequeño vacío.
Cita especímenes y características diagnósticas concretas del Registro de investigación y las usa con precisión para justificar la clasificación.
No intenta razonar por qué el tipo de célula pesa más que el modo de nutrición.
Indica una conclusión pero no explica por qué.
Explica por qué, con un vacío en la lógica científica.
Explica por completo y correctamente por qué el tipo de célula (procariota frente a eucariota), y no el modo de nutrición, es la evidencia decisiva.
Frases confusas o ausentes; sin términos científicos.
Comprensible pero con frases poco claras o sin términos clave.
Frases claras y bien construidas usando vocabulario científico correcto (por ejemplo, 'procariota', 'eucariota', 'heterótrofo').
